glossary.definition: A managed system gradually differing from its approved configuration baseline because of changes, updates, or unauthorized modifications.
Software stored on or close to hardware that controls how the device operates.
A user or workload device such as a laptop, server, phone, or virtual machine that connects to an environment.
Event and measurement data collected from systems, applications, identities, or networks for monitoring and analysis.
The observed security state of a device or identity, such as patch level, configuration, or policy compliance.
A system that receives a request on behalf of a client and forwards it to another destination, often applying policy or inspection.
A service that stores and organizes identity-related objects such as users, groups, devices, and attributes.
A statement from an identity system about authentication or identity attributes that another system may trust.
Something a claimant uses to prove control of an authentication factor, such as a security key, enrolled device, or password.
The amount of systems, data, or users that can be affected when a failure or compromise occurs.
The application data carried inside a packet or message, separate from routing or protocol metadata.
Linking events from different sources or times because they appear related to the same activity.
A defensive destination used to redirect selected network or DNS traffic so access is blocked or observed safely.
Authentication verifies identity, authorization decides allowed actions, and accounting records relevant access activity.
An intermediate form of program instructions produced from source code and executed or translated by a runtime or virtual machine.
Structured so software can parse and process the information automatically instead of relying only on human reading.
A security boundary in which identities, authentication, and access policies are managed under a common authority.
Allowing one application to receive limited permission to act on a user's behalf without receiving the user's password.
Digital information that may be relevant to an investigation or legal matter, such as email, documents, chats, logs, or database records.
Examining the detailed fields, messages, and behavior defined by a network protocol rather than only high-level connection summaries.

authoring_notes: Authored against CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0 and the existing Domain 4 question bundle. Every concept defined in the Domain 4 question bundle is taught exactly once before retrieval practice. Primary cards are definition-first; second reveals use the interaction style that best fits the concept (sequence for processes, comparison/table for commonly confused technologies, and short action/look-for lists for operational decisions). Tables stay compact for mobile use. Glossary entries explain supporting vocabulary, not the main concept of the card. Current NIST guidance is used where it clarifies modern practice; when Security+ terminology differs from current operational guidance, the exam terminology is retained and the nuance is stated explicitly.

Helps detect modification after signing.

reveal.text: Sanitization makes target data infeasible to recover at the required assurance level. Use approved destruction when the media will not be reused or when sanitization cannot provide sufficient assurance.

nodes.title: Legal hold and chain of custody

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about legal hold and chain of custody?

reveal.text: A legal hold preserves potentially relevant information by suspending normal deletion. Chain of custody records who possessed, transferred, stored, or handled evidence and when.

spans.text: who possessed, transferred, stored, or handled evidence and when

prompts.label: PRESERVE + DOCUMENT
prompts.placeholder: Two legal/evidence concepts.

columns.title: Legal hold
items: Suspends normal deletion or destruction for information that may be relevant to litigation or investigation.

columns.title: Chain of custody
items: Documents who collected, possessed, transferred, stored, or handled evidence and when.

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about acquisition, preservation, reporting, and e-discovery?

reveal.text: E-discovery covers identifying, preserving, acquiring, processing, reviewing, and producing electronically stored information for legal or investigative needs, with clear reporting and preservation controls.

spans.text: identifying, preserving, acquiring, processing, reviewing, and producing

prompts.label: FROM COLLECTION TO PRODUCTION
prompts.placeholder: What can e-discovery require?

items: Identify potentially relevant electronically stored information.
Preserve it so normal retention or deletion does not destroy it.
Acquire and process data using defensible methods.
Review and report findings or produce required material according to legal/process requirements.

modules.title: Investigate with the right data sources

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about investigation log sources?

reveal.text: Investigations may use firewall logs, application logs, endpoint logs, OS-specific security logs, IDS/IPS logs, and other network logs. Correlating sources usually provides stronger evidence than relying on one.

spans.text: firewall logs, application logs, endpoint logs

prompts.label: ASK THE SOURCE THAT CAN ANSWER
prompts.placeholder: Different logs tell different parts of the story.

cells.question: Who connected to whom, through which ports/protocols, and what was allowed or blocked?
What did the application or API do for a user/request?
What happened on the host: authentication, process, policy, or security events?
What suspicious network patterns or signatures were detected?

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about investigation metadata?

reveal.text: Metadata such as timestamps, addresses, identities, session information, and file attributes adds context that helps connect events and build an investigation timeline.

spans.text: timestamps, addresses, identities, session information, and file attributes

prompts.label: CONTEXT BUILDS THE TIMELINE
prompts.placeholder: Metadata can connect otherwise separate events.

items: Timestamps and time-zone context.
Source and destination addresses or identifiers.
User, host, process, and session identifiers.
File names, hashes, sizes, owners, or other attributes.
Reliable time synchronization makes cross-source correlation much stronger.

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about scans, automated reports, and dashboards?

reveal.text: Vulnerability scans provide technical findings, automated reports package results for review, and dashboards summarize current status, trends, or priorities.

spans.text: summarize current status, trends, or priorities

prompts.label: RAW FINDING → PACKAGED VIEW
prompts.placeholder: Know the level of abstraction.

cells.purpose: Underlying technical findings about potential weaknesses.
Packaged results for a defined audience, schedule, or workflow.
Current summary, status, trends, or prioritized metrics for quick review.

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What should I know about packet captures?

reveal.text: A packet capture records network packets for protocol-level investigation. It can provide details that flow summaries or ordinary logs do not contain, but may also capture sensitive data.

prompts.label: PACKETS, NOT JUST SUMMARIES
prompts.placeholder: When is a PCAP useful?

items: When flow records show a connection but not enough protocol detail.
When you need packet headers and, when captured and permitted, payload-level evidence.
For protocol troubleshooting, sequence reconstruction, or validating suspicious communications.
Packet captures can contain sensitive data, so collection and retention need controls.
